title: How Pain Works
summary: Josh and Chuck continue their exploration of pain as an umbrella topic. They cover the IASP definition of pain (an unpleasant sensory and emotional experience tied to actual or potential tissue damage), types of pain (acute, chronic, nociceptive, neuropathic, psychogenic), the difference between nociception and pain, Descartes' view of pain as internal, the ascending and descending pain pathways through the spinal cord, thalamus and brain, nociceptors (mechanical, chemical, thermal), A-delta and C fibers, referred pain, the spinal reflex loop, and the fight-or-flight response to pain. They discuss factors that modulate pain (age, gender, culture, memory, attention, fear, emotion), gate control theory by Melzack and Wall, and how pain is managed through NSAIDs, opioids, adjuvant drugs, surgery, TENS units, placebo, mirror therapy and mindfulness. Tangents include cardiologist screenings and a listener email about beavers in Las Vegas.

segments.title: Opening banter and pain as an evolutionary signal
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck introduce the episode as part of a return to umbrella topics, after earlier episodes on pain scales and perceiving pain. They describe pain as an evolutionary signal that prompts an animal to move away from harm.

segments.title: Defining pain and the role of subjectivity
segments.summary: Pain is the most common reason people seek medical attention, and it is fully subjective. The hosts discuss the IASP definition from 1973 and its 2020 revision, which includes the caveat about tissue damage and the role of emotion.

segments.title: Types of pain: acute, nociceptive, neuropathic, chronic
segments.summary: The hosts describe acute pain and its protective function, nociceptive pain from tissue damage (including cancer pain), and neuropathic pain from nerve damage such as sciatica and multiple sclerosis. They explain chronic pain as lasting six months or longer, and mention psychogenic chronic pain with no clear physical cause. Chuck shares a personal story about hitting his shin.

segments.title: Nociception versus pain and Descartes
segments.summary: Nociception, the sensing of noxious stimuli by nociceptors, is distinct from the experience of pain, which is the brain's response. The hosts note that the two can exist separately, and that Descartes in the 1600s proposed an internal process, while earlier thinkers saw pain as external or punishment. They also cover the ascending and descending signal pathways.

segments.title: Brain as the source of pain and burns
segments.summary: The hosts discuss Ramachandran's view that pain is the brain's opinion of the body's state. They describe burns, sensitized nerves, and cuts that may not hurt, and how the brain integrates information, using hangnails and paper cuts as examples.

segments.title: Nociceptor types and A-delta and C fibers
segments.summary: Nociceptors are tuned to mechanical, chemical, and thermal stimuli. A-delta fibers are myelinated and fast, producing the initial sharp pain, while C fibers are unmyelinated and slower, producing the follow-up burning or throbbing. Inflammatory chemicals released from damaged cells also contribute to the signal.

segments.title: Referred pain and the path of the pain signal to the brain
segments.summary: Pain signals travel to spinal gray matter, then up the spinal white matter, through the medulla and thalamus, to the somatosensory cortex. Referred pain explains why pain can be felt in other parts of the body, such as heart attack pain in the arm and brain freeze. A pinball analogy is used. The spinal reflex loop can trigger withdrawal before the brain registers pain, and pain can activate fight, flight or freeze.

segments.title: Brain involvement and distraction
segments.summary: The hosts discuss evidence that the brain is involved in pain, including delayed hand movements and the Fight Club scene where the character distracts himself with a penguin image. Descending pathways from the brain can overpower ascending signals.

segments.title: Recommendations and off-topic chat
segments.summary: The hosts talk about a Netflix movie and the horror movies they have seen. This is largely off-topic conversation rather than a sponsor read.

segments.title: Factors that influence pain: age, gender, culture, memory, needles, emotion
segments.summary: The hosts describe how age, gender, culture, memory of past pain, watching a needle, and emotion affect pain experience. They cover gate control theory by Melzack and Wall, the faulty sensor analogy from Atul Gawande, and the treatments: NSAIDs, opioids, non-pain drugs, surgery, TENS units, alternative therapies, placebo, mirror therapy, and mindfulness. A listener email about beavers in Las Vegas closes the episode.
